draft.title: The budgeted balance sheet
card: A budgeted balance sheet estimates the assets, liabilities and owner's equity a business expects to have on one date, the end of the coming period.
It starts from the closing balances of the last actual balance sheet. The budgeted cash flow statement and budgeted income statement then show the changes to each item.
Cash comes from the closing balance in the budgeted cash flow statement. Owner's equity is the opening equity, plus budgeted profit and capital contributed, less drawings.
The accounting equation must still hold: assets = liabilities + owner's equity. If the totals differ, there is an error in the budget.
draft.remember: A budgeted balance sheet is a forecast of the business's position on one future date, and it must balance.

a.q: What does a budgeted balance sheet estimate?
opts: The assets, liabilities and equity at the end of the period
The revenue and expenses earned over the coming period
The cash received and paid out during the coming period
The difference between budgeted and actual results
a.why: A balance sheet shows the position on one date, so the budgeted version estimates the position at the end of the coming period. Revenue and expenses belong to the income statement, and cash receipts and payments belong to the cash flow statement.
a.clue: A balance sheet is a snapshot on one date, not a record over time.

b.q: Priya's Pet Supplies has opening equity of $80 000. For the coming year, it budgets a profit of $30 000 and drawings of $12 000, with no new capital. What is the budgeted closing equity?
b.why: Closing equity = opening equity + profit - drawings = $80 000 + $30 000 - $12 000 = $98 000. Adding the drawings instead of taking them away gives $110 000, but drawings reduce the owner's equity.
b.clue: Profit adds to equity and drawings take away from it.

a.best: The assets, liabilities and equity at the end of the period

problems.detail: The why says adding the drawings instead of taking them away gives $110 000. That is wrong: $80 000 + $30 000 + $12 000 = $122 000. The $110 000 distractor comes from ignoring drawings ($80 000 + $30 000), so the explanation misdescribes the mistake.

check.summary: The card and both questions are correct. The explanation for (b) gets its arithmetic wrong: $110 000 comes from ignoring drawings, not from adding them, which would give $122 000.
